topic: Christianity / Islam / Judaism / Buddhism / Hinduism / Sikhism: Social & Historical Developments
subject: religious-studies

items.q: What does karma mean in Hindu and Buddhist thought?
items.correct: The principle that actions have moral consequences shaping future experience or rebirth — not fate, but ethical cause and effect built into reality.
items.misconception: Karma is when bad things happen to bad people as punishment.
items.random_wrong: Karma is a god who decides what happens to you.
items.why: Students treat karma as cosmic justice meted out by a deity. In its philosophical origins it is impersonal moral causation — your own actions, not external judgement, shape your circumstances.

items.q: What is the doctrine of the Trinity?
items.correct: God is one being existing in three persons (Father, Son, Holy Spirit) — distinct in person but united in essence; Christians remain monotheistic.
items.misconception: Christians believe in three different gods.
items.random_wrong: The Trinity refers to heaven, earth and hell.
items.why: Students treat 'three persons' as 'three gods'. The orthodox position is one God in three distinct persons sharing one substance — a notoriously difficult concept students often misrepresent as polytheism.

items.q: What is the difference between Sunni and Shia Islam?
items.correct: They split over who should lead the Muslim community after Muhammad: Sunnis accepted Abu Bakr and elected caliphs; Shias believed leadership should follow Muhammad's bloodline through Ali.
items.misconception: Sunnis and Shias believe in different gods.
items.random_wrong: Sunnis follow the Quran and Shias follow the Bible.
items.why: Both share the Quran, prophet and core beliefs. The original split was political — about succession — and theological differences developed later. Students inflate it into a different religion.

items.q: Did Luther set out to found a new church in 1517?
items.correct: No — the 95 Theses called for debate and reform of abuses (especially indulgences) within the Catholic Church; separation followed later, after condemnation and excommunication.
items.misconception: Luther nailed up the 95 Theses to announce the founding of the Lutheran Church.
items.random_wrong: Luther's 95 Theses were a list of new books to add to the Bible.
items.why: Luther was excommunicated in 1521, years after 1517. Reading the Reformation's outcome back into its beginning misses how reform movements escalate — a key point in church history questions.

items.q: Was the Great Schism of 1054 part of the Protestant Reformation?
items.correct: No — 1054 split the Eastern Orthodox and Western Catholic churches over issues like the filioque and papal authority; the Reformation (from 1517) divided the Western church itself.
items.misconception: The Great Schism of 1054 happened when Luther broke away from the Catholic Church.
items.random_wrong: The Great Schism was the division between Sunni and Shia Islam.
items.why: Two separate divisions, five centuries apart: East-West (1054), then within the West (16th century). Students merge them into one 'church split', losing the chronology examiners expect.

items.q: When was the Trinity affirmed by council?
items.why: Correct answer: AD 325. “AD 33” sounds right because it borrows the language of the topic — but it fails this question. Re-read the notes on why.

items.q: Who developed the doctrine of original sin?
items.why: It's Augustine. “Aquinas” is the classic near-miss here; knowing why it's wrong is worth as much as knowing the right answer.

items.q: On what day did Jesus rise according to Christians?
items.why: The real figure is 3 day. The wrong options cluster deliberately close — anchor the exact number to one concrete fact so it can't drift.
